Posterior summaries of the diagnostics

Source: vignettes/posterior-summaries.Rmd
posterior-summaries.Rmd

reliability_posterior() reports a posterior mean and a 95% posterior interval for each diagnostic, and the posterior probability that the informativeness II exceeds 1/2. In this vignette we explain where these numbers come from and which choices lie behind them. We start with the model and its prior, compare a posterior mean with a plug-in value, and explain the interval for the dispersion HH. We then come back to the prior for trials with few sites, and end with posterior draws, for summaries that the package does not compute. Our examples are the eight schools of Rubin (1981) and the passing outcome of the Online Credit Recovery Study (Rickles et al. 2024).

library(poolinfo)

The model and the prior

We work with the normal hierarchical model in which site jj’s estimate τ̂j\hat\tau_j has a known sampling variance vjv_j,

τ̂j∣τj∼N(τj,vj),τj∼N(μ,στ2),j=1,…,J, \hat\tau_j \mid \tau_j \sim N(\tau_j, v_j), \qquad \tau_j \sim N(\mu, \sigma_\tau^2), \qquad j = 1, \dots, J,

independently over sites. By default the prior is flat on the mean μ\mu and on the between-site standard deviation στ\sigma_\tau. A prior flat on στ\sigma_\tau is not flat on the variance. As a density in στ2\sigma_\tau^2 it is proportional to 1/στ1/\sigma_\tau, so it puts less weight on large variances than a flat prior on στ2\sigma_\tau^2 would (Gelman 2006). Integrating μ\mu out leaves a posterior for στ\sigma_\tau alone, known up to a constant, and vignette("implementation") gives its formula. Every diagnostic depends only on στ\sigma_\tau and the vjv_j, so its posterior mean, its quantiles and the probability that it exceeds a value are one-dimensional integrals over that posterior. Because the package computes them by quadrature rather than simulation, they have no Monte Carlo error.

Our first example, eight_schools, has the estimated effects of coaching on the SAT-V in eight schools, with their standard errors. We fit the posterior.

schools <- reliability_posterior(estimate, se = se, site = school,
                                 data = eight_schools,
                                 scale_label = "SAT-V point")
schools
#> Reliability profile of 8 sites (posterior)
#> Model: estimate ~ N(effect, se^2), effect ~ N(mean, sigma_tau^2),
#>        sites independent
#> Prior: flat on the mean and on sigma_tau
#> Scale of the effects: SAT-V point
#> Summaries are conditional on the supplied standard errors.
#> Each site counts equally in the diagnostics, whatever its size.
#> 
#>                              mean     95% interval
#>   informativeness I          0.225    0.000    0.745
#>   mean reliability           0.230    0.000    0.735
#>   dispersion H               0.0143   0.0000   0.0283
#>   concentration count J_eff  7.2      6.8      7.9      of 8
#>   logit variance V           0.230    (fixed by the standard errors)
#>   sigma_tau                  6.58     0.243    20.8
#>   effect mean                7.93     -2.09    18.2
#> 
#>   Pr(I > 0.5)                0.138
#>   I at E(sigma_tau^2)        0.338

The posterior of στ\sigma_\tau is wide. Its 95% interval runs from 0.24 to 20.8 SAT-V points, and the interval for II runs from 0.00 to 0.75.

In the last block, Pr(I > 0.5) is the posterior probability that στ2\sigma_\tau^2 exceeds GM(v)\mathrm{GM}(v), the geometric mean of the sampling variances. The threshold 1/2 is where the leading term of S‾−I\bar S - I changes sign (Lee 2026, Proposition 2), as vignette("poolinfo") explains.

plot_sigma_scale() plots the posterior density of στ\sigma_\tau with a second axis for II, and shades the region where II exceeds 1/2.

plot_sigma_scale(schools)

The density is highest at 0 and falls steadily. The shading starts at στ=GM(v)=12.1\sigma_\tau = \sqrt{\mathrm{GM}(v)} = 12.1 points, where I=1/2I = 1/2, and 0.138 of the probability lies beyond it. Because II increases with στ\sigma_\tau, each quantile of II is II at the same quantile of στ\sigma_\tau, which the top axis lets you read off.

Posterior means and plug-in values

The printed fit gives the posterior mean of II in its first row and, in its last line, II at the posterior mean of στ2\sigma_\tau^2. That is the value you would get by putting this estimate of στ2\sigma_\tau^2 into the formula for II. plugin_gap() gives both, and their difference, for four diagnostics.

print(plugin_gap(schools), digits = 3)
#>   functional posterior_mean at_mean_sigma2 difference
#> 1          I         0.2253         0.3379     0.1126
#> 2       mean         0.2297         0.3464     0.1167
#> 3          H         0.0143         0.0249     0.0106
#> 4      J_eff         7.1700         7.3631     0.1930

For the eight schools the two values of II are far apart, 0.225 against 0.338. The posterior mean averages II over the values of στ\sigma_\tau that the data allow. The plug-in value first averages στ2\sigma_\tau^2 and then applies II, and the long right tail pulls the posterior mean of στ2\sigma_\tau^2, 75.2, far above its median, 27.4. Whatever the data, II is a concave function of στ2\sigma_\tau^2. By Jensen’s inequality, then, its posterior mean is at most its value at the posterior mean of στ2\sigma_\tau^2, with equality only when the posterior of στ2\sigma_\tau^2 is a point mass (Lee 2026, Proposition 3). The same holds for every SjS_j, and so for S‾\bar S.

Proposition 3 gives no such order for HH and JeffJ_{\mathrm{eff}}, and the positive differences in their rows are a property of these data. For the passing outcome of the credit recovery study, with 32 sites, the difference for HH is negative.

passing <- reliability_posterior(estimate, se = se, data = ocrs)
print(plugin_gap(passing), digits = 3)
#>   functional posterior_mean at_mean_sigma2 difference
#> 1          I         0.6709         0.6911   2.02e-02
#> 2       mean         0.6635         0.6823   1.88e-02
#> 3          H         0.0253         0.0253  -2.04e-05
#> 4      J_eff        31.1704        31.2816   1.11e-01

Here II and S‾\bar S again come out larger at the posterior mean of στ2\sigma_\tau^2, as they must, while HH comes out smaller, by 2.0e-05.

A third number is common in practice, II at a point estimate of στ2\sigma_\tau^2 such as the REML estimate. For the eight schools that estimate is 0, which makes every reliability 0. reliability_profile() computes the profile at any value of στ\sigma_\tau, or at the estimate of a metafor fit, but such a profile carries no uncertainty about στ\sigma_\tau.

Intervals

The posterior intervals are central, with 2.5% of the posterior probability below the lower end and 2.5% above the upper end. We use central intervals because they carry over through increasing functions. II, S‾\bar S and JeffJ_{\mathrm{eff}} increase with στ\sigma_\tau, so the ends of their intervals are their values at the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of στ\sigma_\tau. A highest-density interval does not carry over in general, since a nonlinear change of scale moves the region of highest density. For the eight schools it would also run from 0, where the density of στ\sigma_\tau is highest, to the 95% quantile.

The dispersion HH needs more care. It is 0 at στ=0\sigma_\tau = 0, peaks where S‾=I\bar S = I, and returns toward 0 as στ\sigma_\tau grows, so each value of HH below the peak comes from two values of στ\sigma_\tau. The package adds the posterior probabilities of the two branches to get the distribution function of HH, and solves it for the quantiles. For the eight schools the interval for HH runs from 0.00004 to 0.02833, just below the largest value that HH can take with these standard errors, 0.02837. The upper end is so close to the largest value because HH is flat near its peak. Every στ\sigma_\tau from 12.1 to 13.1 points gives a value of HH above the upper end, and these values of στ\sigma_\tau carry the remaining 2.5% of the probability.

functional_density() returns the posterior density of a diagnostic on a grid, by a change of variables from the density of στ\sigma_\tau, and plot_functionals() plots it with the posterior mean, the plug-in value and the 95% interval.

plot_functionals(schools)

The solid line marks the posterior mean of II, 0.225, the dashed line the plug-in value, 0.338, and the shading the interval up to 0.75. Near I=0I = 0 the density is unbounded, and the plot cuts its vertical axis. Under the flat prior, as under every prior that sd_prior() offers, the posterior density of στ\sigma_\tau is positive at 0. Close to 0 the informativeness is nearly στ2/GM(v)\sigma_\tau^2/\mathrm{GM}(v), so the density of II grows like I−1/2I^{-1/2} as II approaches 0. A gray line marks the threshold 1/2.

prob_above() computes the posterior probability that II, S‾\bar S, JeffJ_{\mathrm{eff}} or στ\sigma_\tau itself exceeds a value. We ask for the probability that στ\sigma_\tau exceeds 5 SAT-V points.

prob_above(schools, threshold = 5, which = "sigma_tau")
#> [1] 0.5194775

It is 0.52, a little over a half.

Few sites and the prior

With few sites the posterior of στ\sigma_\tau is wide, and the prior matters. Under the flat prior, the package’s default and the prior of Lee (2026), the posterior is proper only with at least 3 sites, the posterior mean of στ\sigma_\tau exists only with at least 4, and that of στ2\sigma_\tau^2 only with at least 5. ?sd_prior gives these counts for a mean model and for the other priors. When a posterior mean does not exist, the printed fit reports it as not defined. We fit the first 4 of the eight schools.

four <- reliability_posterior(estimate, se = se, data = eight_schools[1:4, ])
four
#> Reliability profile of 4 sites (posterior)
#> Model: estimate ~ N(effect, se^2), effect ~ N(mean, sigma_tau^2),
#>        sites independent
#> Prior: flat on the mean and on sigma_tau
#> Summaries are conditional on the supplied standard errors.
#> Each site counts equally in the diagnostics, whatever its size.
#> 
#>                              mean     95% interval
#>   informativeness I          0.439    0.001    0.976
#>   mean reliability           0.439    0.001    0.975
#>   dispersion H               0.0112   0.0001   0.0197
#>   concentration count J_eff  3.8      3.5      4.0      of 4
#>   logit variance V           0.159    (fixed by the standard errors)
#>   sigma_tau                  18.7     0.465    82.0
#>   effect mean                9.71     -18.6    38.5
#> 
#>   Pr(I > 0.5)                0.437
#>   I at E(sigma_tau^2)        not defined: E(sigma_tau^2) does not exist with 4 sites

The posterior mean of II is now 0.44, against 0.23 with all 8 schools, and the 95% interval of στ\sigma_\tau reaches 82 points. For both sets the REML estimate of στ\sigma_\tau is 0, but four schools say less about στ\sigma_\tau than eight. Under the flat prior the posterior density of στ\sigma_\tau falls off like στ1−J\sigma_\tau^{1-J}, slowly when J=4J = 4, and the posterior probability that στ\sigma_\tau exceeds 20 points is 0.27 with 4 schools against 0.03 with 8. The posterior mean of στ2\sigma_\tau^2 does not exist with 4 sites, so the printout has no plug-in value. Under a half-normal prior with scale 10 the two sets differ as well, with posterior means of II of 0.20 and 0.16.

Proper priors on στ\sigma_\tau are a common alternative when there are few sites, such as half-normal or half-t priors with a scale on the scale of the effects (Gelman 2006). sd_prior() makes them, and prior_sensitivity() refits a posterior under each and collects the fits:

prior_sensitivity(schools, list(
  `half-normal, scale 10` = sd_prior("half_normal", scale = 10),
  `half-t, scale 10, 3 df` = sd_prior("half_t", scale = 10, df = 3),
  `half-Cauchy, scale 5` = sd_prior("half_cauchy", scale = 5)
))
#> Comparison of 4 analyses
#> Intervals are central posterior intervals.
#> Each analysis is conditional on its own standard errors.
#> 
#>   analysis                J  informativeness I     mean reliability
#>   flat                    8  0.225 [0.000, 0.745]  0.230
#>   half-normal, scale 10   8  0.157 [0.000, 0.570]  0.162
#>   half-t, scale 10, 3 df  8  0.156 [0.000, 0.587]  0.161
#>   half-Cauchy, scale 5    8  0.105 [0.000, 0.497]  0.110
#> 
#>   analysis                dispersion H             concentration count J_eff
#>   flat                    0.0143 [0.0000, 0.0283]  7.2
#>   half-normal, scale 10   0.0118 [0.0000, 0.0282]  7.1
#>   half-t, scale 10, 3 df  0.0116 [0.0000, 0.0282]  7.1
#>   half-Cauchy, scale 5    0.0084 [0.0000, 0.0278]  7.0

All three put more weight on small values of στ\sigma_\tau than the flat prior does. They pull the posterior mean of II down from 0.23 to between 0.11 and 0.16, and the interval’s upper end from 0.75 to between 0.50 and 0.59. We would name the prior in any report on a trial this small, and show the fits under more than one.

A given prior matters less as the number of sites grows. To see this with the trial and the scale of the effects held fixed, we refit the passing outcome in its 13 Algebra 1 sites, its 19 English 9 sites and all 32 sites, each under two half-normal priors. A scale of 0.1 is about 0.8 times the geometric-mean standard error GM(v)\sqrt{\mathrm{GM}(v)} in each set, as the scale 10 is for the eight schools. A scale of 0.5, a between-site standard deviation of 50 percentage points, is far beyond any plausible spread of effects on passing, so that prior is weak. For each set we compute how far each prior moves the posterior mean of II from its value under the flat prior.

half_normal <- list(`scale 0.1` = sd_prior("half_normal", scale = 0.1),
                    `scale 0.5` = sd_prior("half_normal", scale = 0.5))
subsets <- list(`Algebra 1` = ocrs[ocrs$subject == "Algebra 1", ],
                `English 9` = ocrs[ocrs$subject == "English 9", ],
                all = ocrs)
shift <- sapply(subsets, function(d) {
  fit <- reliability_posterior(estimate, se = se, data = d)
  I <- as.data.frame(prior_sensitivity(fit, half_normal))$I
  setNames(I[-1] - I[1], names(half_normal))
})
data.frame(sites = sapply(subsets, nrow), round(t(shift), 3),
           check.names = FALSE)
#>           sites scale 0.1 scale 0.5
#> Algebra 1    13    -0.118    -0.007
#> English 9    19    -0.072    -0.004
#> all          32    -0.045    -0.002

Under the prior with scale 0.1 the posterior mean of II falls by 0.118 with 13 sites, 0.072 with 19 and 0.045 with 32. Under the weak prior it falls by 0.007 or less. So a weak prior hardly matters with 32 sites, but a prior with a scale near the standard errors still moves II by about half of its posterior standard deviation, 0.081.

Draws

Some summaries need posterior draws, for example those that involve several site effects at once. profile_draws() draws στ\sigma_\tau by inverting its posterior distribution function, then the mean given στ\sigma_\tau, and, with sites = TRUE, the site effects given both. With seed the draws are reproducible, and the session’s random number generator is left as it was. We use draws to find the posterior probability that school A, whose estimate is the largest, also has the largest effect:

draws <- profile_draws(schools, ndraws = 4000, seed = 1, sites = TRUE)
effects <- draws[, paste0("effect_", eight_schools$school)]
top_A <- mean(apply(effects, 1, which.max) == 1)
round(c(probability = top_A,
        mcse = sqrt(top_A * (1 - top_A) / nrow(draws))), 4)
#> probability        mcse 
#>      0.2585      0.0069

School A has the largest effect in 26% of the draws, more often than any other school but far from always, because the model pulls the eight effects toward one another. The draws are independent, so the Monte Carlo standard error of this proportion is the binomial one, 0.007. Four times as many draws would halve it.

Draws from other software go to reliability_draws(), which computes the diagnostics at each draw of στ\sigma_\tau and reports their Monte Carlo standard errors. It reads a brms fit of this model directly, and vignette("implementation") has an example.

Integration checks

The numerical integration is checked as each fit is made, and check_numerics() shows the results. If a check falls outside its limit, reliability_posterior() warns as it builds the fit. vignette("implementation") explains the checks and the other method of integration, posterior_control(engine = "adaptive").

References

Gelman, Andrew. 2006. “Prior Distributions for Variance Parameters in Hierarchical Models (Comment on Article by Browne and Draper).” Bayesian Analysis 1 (3): 515–34. https://doi.org/10.1214/06-BA117A.

Rickles, Jordan, Margaret Clements, Iliana Brodziak de los Reyes, Mark Lachowicz, Shuqiong Lin, and Jessica Heppen. 2024. “A Multisite Randomized Study of an Online Learning Approach to High School Credit Recovery: Effects on Student Experiences and Proximal Outcomes.” Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness 17 (3): 467–90. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2023.2198524.
Rubin, Donald B. 1981. “Estimation in Parallel Randomized Experiments.” Journal of Educational Statistics 6 (4): 377–401. https://doi.org/10.3102/10769986006004377.
